title: Historical introduction to Etruria
paras: Central Italy, 9th-1st centuries BC

Etruria was the first great civilisation of the Italian peninsula and developed between the 9th and 1st centuries BC, from the Villanovan period (the beginning of the first Italian iron metallurgy) to the Romano-Etruscan phase, in central Italy, over the present-day regions of Tuscany, Lazio and Umbria.

The Etruscans never formed a unitary state, since they were organised into twelve city-states, governed first by kings or great lords and later by magistrates (citizens holding public office) drawn from the aristocracy. Hence the description of a highly polarised society, probably without middle classes.
The Etruscans held sway over the early Romans for a century, between 616 and 509 BC. However, Rome later absorbed the Etruscan cities, bringing Etruscan independence to an end in 264 BC.

title: Characteristics of Etruscan sport
paras: Tarquinia, c. 550-400 BC

Sport held a very important place in Etruscan society, which had a deep-rooted physical culture, as shown by the musculature and the athletic bearing of the bodies depicted in its art. Nevertheless, there are no exact data on the specific systems of physical education.

The Etruscans left no text about their games, so their sport is known from the outside. What we know comes from a few Greek and Latin texts, from a small number of inscriptions but, above all, from images and iconography, which are the main source of knowledge.

Among these images, certain tombs painted with sporting scenes stand out, something very rare in Antiquity beyond Egypt. Even so, there were few of them. Of the some six thousand tombs in the necropolis of Tarquinia, only about two hundred bear paintings (around 3%), since decoration was an expensive practice that only very few families could afford. What is interesting is that seventeen of them, dated between 530 and 450 BC, have been recorded as showing sporting games.

These paintings depict, as studies agree, the funeral games held in honour of the noble deceased who occupies the tomb, like those at the funeral of Patroclus in the Iliad. Painting them on the wall also ensured that the rite was repeated for ever and prolonged its commemorative effect.
Many of the athletes depicted would have been professionals in the service of the aristocracy, although the labels in the Tomb of the Inscriptions associate some horsemen with noble families.

title: Etruscan women
paras: Tarquinia, c. 500 BC

The Etruscan woman enjoyed greater freedom than the Greek woman and than the Roman woman would later have, since she took part in feasts and banquets, sometimes as a dancer (right-hand image), and attended sporting events as a spectator.

The Tomb of the Bigae at Tarquinia (image below), painted c. 500 BC, shows spectators of noble origin seated on wooden stands covered with awnings. Men and women appear mixed together while the chariots parade before them ahead of the race. In the front row of the stand a woman raises her arm towards the charioteers, a gesture that has been read as a greeting or as the starting signal.
As for practice, there is no evidence that women competed in organised sport, since in the paintings they are never seen taking part in a competition.

title: A clear Greek inspiration
paras: Italy and the Mediterranean, 8th-5th centuries BC
Etruscan sporting scenes closely match the sporting motifs of the great Greek festivals, since Greek sport reached Italy from the south.
From the mid-8th century BC the Greeks founded cities in southern Italy and Sicily, where citizens trained and prepared their bodies to go to Olympia, just as happened in mainland Greece.

Another channel of exchange was the trade in objects. Etruscan tombs are full of Panathenaic amphorae, the prizes of the games of Athens, like the one in the right-hand image, which reached Etruria as an imported luxury.

The Etruscans also knew the Greek sanctuaries, since they visited them in person. Etruscan gifts have been found at Delphi, and an Etruscan king was the first foreigner to make an offering to Zeus at Olympia, although there is no evidence that any Etruscan competed in the Greek games.

title: Athletics, wrestling and boxing
paras: The Etruscans took over a large part of the Greek events, although they introduced some modifications of a local nature.

Athletics. The Etruscans appear practising many Olympic events, such as running, discus throwing, javelin or the long jump with halteres. A figure in the Tomb of the Bigae has also been read as a pole vault, one of the earliest depictions of this discipline. What was being jumped over is unknown, although Thuillier (1985) believes that the pole might have served to vault over a horse.
Tarquinia, 6th-5th centuries BC

Wrestling and boxing. They combined Greek influence with a tradition of their own, since there were already Etruscan boxers in the 7th century BC. Boxing was a sport much admired by the Etruscans, and it almost always appears accompanied by a flute player, who according to Thuillier (2013) set the rhythm of the fight, something Greek authors took as a sign of softness. The depictions show well-trained wrestlers with highly developed musculature. In the Tomb of the Augurs (image below) two wrestlers compete for three bronze cauldrons at their feet, which would have been the prize for the winner.

title: Aquatic activities
paras: Tarquinia, late 6th century BC

In the Tomb of Hunting and Fishing at Tarquinia, one of the most famous in the necropolis, a youth dives headfirst into the sea from a rock or stone structure, while another climbs up it (image). The scene was painted at the end of the 6th century BC.
The meaning of the dive is debated. Scholars concentrate on three main hypotheses.
Religious hypothesis. The passage of the soul of the deceased from the world of the living to the afterlife, through the body's entry into the depth and darkness of the water (Bellia, 2014).
Ritual hypothesis. A physical practice of elite youths that marked their coming of age, showing their courage by jumping from a high and risky position (Hölscher, 2022).
Simplest hypothesis. It would merely show young people enjoying themselves and spending some leisure time in the water (Thuillier, 1985).

Be that as it may, the Etruscans were a people who mastered the aquatic environment. They were seafarers, devoted to trade, fishing and, according to Greek authors, piracy, so swimming may well have been a common practice among them. Even so, no Etruscan document allows us to speak of competitions in the water.

title: Etruscan chariot racing
paras: Chiusi and Tarquinia, 6th-5th centuries BC

Chariot racing was one of the favourite activities of the Etruscans. The number of depictions points to a preference for bigae over quadrigae, although they also used the triga, the three-horse chariot.

The Etruscan charioteer differed from the Greek one in three ways. He tied the reins around his waist, which multiplied the risk in the event of an accident, but allowed him to drive with one hand. With the other he wielded the whip, instead of the long goad with which the Greek urged on the horses. Finally, he wore a short tunic and a helmet, as opposed to the long tunic and bare head of the Greek charioteer.

The social origin of the charioteers is disputed. Crowther and Kyle consider them to be of servile origin (cited in Banducci, 2014) and Thuillier (1985), low-ranking professionals dependent on a lord.

The audience was the aristocracy, and since keeping horses and charioteers was very expensive, the race served as an excuse to display the wealth of whoever paid for it and organised the competitions. What Etruscan art dwells on again and again is the crash. It shows overturned chariots and charioteers thrown through the air, which for the public must have been the most exciting moment, something that anticipates the taste for violence in sport that the Romans would inherit.

title: Horse racing and the troia
paras: Murlo and Tragliatella, 7th-6th centuries BC

Horse races with riders are somewhat less numerous in Etruscan art, so their importance must have been lower than that of chariot races. The image shows an Etruscan bit of c. 700-650 BC, the metal piece placed in the horse's mouth which, joined to the reins, makes it possible to guide the mount.
One novelty was the introduction of acrobatic variants such as the desultores, riders who leapt from one horse to another in mid-race or performed risky balancing acts on horseback.
The troia was another equestrian discipline, a game of skill on horseback in which the riders followed a labyrinth of curves, as shown by the jug from the 7th century BC in the image.

title: The phersu
paras: The Tomb of the Augurs at Tarquinia, painted c. 530 BC, shows a masked figure with his name written above his head, the phersu, which probably means «mask» and is related to the Latin persona. The phersu sets a dog on a hooded man who holds a club to defend himself, but the rope held by the masked figure prevents him from saving his life.

The meaning of the scene remains open. Thuillier (1985) sees the phersu as an executioner putting a condemned man to death, in a punishment closer to condemnation to the beasts than to gladiatorial combat.

Avramidou (2009), on the other hand, interprets it as the staging of an Orphic rite, with the masked figure in the role of Orpheus and the dog in that of Cerberus. Orpheus was the musician of Greek mythology who went down to the world of the dead to rescue his wife, and Cerberus the three-headed dog that guarded its entrance, so the scene would represent the passage of the soul of the deceased to the world of the dead.

For a long time this scene was regarded as the direct precedent of gladiatorial games. However, none of the seventeen paintings of funeral games from Tarquinia and Chiusi shows a single gladiator, and gladiatorial combat did not reach Etruria until the late 4th or early 3rd century BC, so the phersu remains, at most, a forerunner of the combats with wild beasts (Kyle, 1998), although it may be a direct precedent for turning the pain, suffering and death of a person fallen into disgrace into public entertainment, which later became popular in the Roman world.

title: Etruscan games
paras: The social life of the Etruscan upper classes included numerous feasts and banquets, and at these gatherings it was customary to play games in which wine took centre stage.

Three of these games stood out. In the ascolia one had to keep one's balance on a greased wineskin (a sheepskin bag), and in the kottabos the last drops in the cup were flung at a target, such as the dish of a candelabrum (right-hand image). People also played dice, probably for stakes.
Nevertheless, these games were only partly Etruscan, since kottabos is documented at the Greek banquet. Dice were also played by aristocratic women.

title: What Rome inherited from Etruria
paras: Etruria and Rome, 7th-3rd centuries BC

Etruscan sport faded out before Etruria itself. Scenes of games disappear from the tombs at the end of the 5th century BC, and the last is that of the Tomb of the Warrior, c. 400 BC, probably because keeping athletes and charioteers was very expensive and the aristocracy had grown poorer.

What Rome received from Etruscan sport was, above all, the preference of the nobility for attending as spectators. In Etruria the aristocracy watched from wooden stands with awnings, like those in the Tomb of the Bigae, and the competing fell to paid professionals. The Roman elites inherited that position, since they shared the sense of shame at performing before the public as professional athletes (Thuillier, 2013).

With that way of watching came the taste for violence. Etruscan art revelled in overturned chariots and, according to Thuillier (1985), the phersu turned the death of a condemned man into a spectacle, so the aristocracy enjoyed the danger faced by others. Rome also kept the triga, the desultores, the troia and the reins tied around the waist, which its charioteers used until the end of the Empire despite the risk in the event of an accident.

title: Historical introduction to Rome
paras: The history of Rome spans more than twelve centuries, from its foundation as a small city in Latium to the fall of the Western Empire. It is usually divided into three stages according to who held power, the Monarchy, the Republic and the Empire, which the timeline sets out beneath the map of the territory that Rome came to rule.

Monarchy (753-509 BC). Tradition places the foundation in 753 BC, although the city grew out of the gradual union of villages of Latins and Sabines on the hills by the Tiber. It was ruled by kings, the last three of them Etruscans, until in 509 BC the aristocracy expelled the last of them, Tarquinius Superbus, whom tradition presents as a tyrant. Today this is understood as a reaction by the great lineages to recover the power the kings had curtailed, at a time when Etruscan rule was receding in Latium.

Republic (509-27 BC). The aristocracy divided the king's power between two consuls elected every year, who could veto each other, so that no one would ever again rule alone. In those centuries Rome conquered Italy and, after defeating Carthage in the Punic Wars, the rest of the Mediterranean. The civil wars of the 1st century BC, in which generals at the head of their own armies fought one another, brought the republican system to an end. The most powerful of them, Julius Caesar, had himself appointed dictator for life and was assassinated in 44 BC.

Empire (27 BC-AD 476). It began with Augustus, Caesar's great-nephew and adopted son, who concentrated all power without abolishing the republican institutions and was the first of more than seventy emperors. At the beginning of the 2nd century AD it reached its greatest extent (see map). On the death of Theodosius, in AD 395, it was divided in two, East and West, because such a vast territory was very difficult to govern from a single centre. The western half, under pressure from the Germanic peoples, fell in AD 476, when a Germanic chieftain deposed the last emperor. The eastern half, with its capital at Constantinople, survived for almost a thousand years more.

title: Governing Rome, from Republic to Empire
paras: Rome, 509 BC-3rd century AD

The chart compares the government of Rome under the Republic (upper half) and under the Empire (lower half), level by level, from supreme power, at the centre, to the people, in the outer ring. At the centre of the Republic were the two consuls, elected every year, and around them the Senate, which brought together for life some 300 former magistrates and decided on war, taxes and the government of the provinces.

The magistrates were the public officials elected to govern Rome, that is, to command the armies, administer justice and run the life of the city. Among them were the aediles, a kind of city councillors, who looked after the markets, the streets and the public buildings and organised the games. Each office was held by at least two people who could veto each other and received no pay, so only the rich could afford to stand. As they were elected every year by the citizens' vote, anyone who aspired to an office needed to win over the people.

In the outer ring, the assemblies brought together male citizens to elect the magistrates and vote on laws, although voting was by groups according to wealth. After a long struggle with the old patrician families, the plebeians also won their own representatives, the tribunes of the plebs, who could veto any magistrate.

Augustus kept these institutions, although he left them without real power. He himself occupied the centre as princeps, «first citizen», for life, with command of all the armies and the powers of the tribunes. The Senate, with some 600 members purged by the emperor, governed only the pacified provinces. The magistrates, now elected by the Senate, kept only the prestige of the title, and positions of trust passed to the equites, the second group of the elite. The assemblies disappeared in the 1st century AD, so the people stopped voting and could make itself heard only in the circus, the theatre and the amphitheatre (Woolf, 2012).

title: The Roman social pyramid
paras: Rome, 2nd century BC-2nd century AD

The previous slide showed the offices of government. The pyramid shows the social groups from which those who held them came, ordered by wealth and rank. At the top, below the emperor, was the senatorial order, the few families that produced the senators and magistrates of Rome, aediles included. Next came the equestrian order, that of the equites, so called because they originally served on horseback in the army. Over time it brought together businessmen and senior administrators, to whom Augustus entrusted the administration and supply of Rome. After them came the notables of each city, who governed their community from the council and the local magistracies and paid for its games and its buildings.

The dashed line separates the powerful from the humble, a boundary that counted before the law: for the same crime, a humble person was punished more harshly, even with death before the wild beasts. The largest group among them was the plebs, the free citizens without fortune, which in Rome received public grain and was the people that filled the circus, the theatre and the amphitheatre.

At the base were the slaves, the property of their masters and without rights. Most were prisoners of war, so slavery did not depend on skin colour, although people were also enslaved for debts or crimes. Manumission, that is, release by the master, turned them into freedmen, citizens of lower rank than the freeborn, although their children were born full citizens.

title: Roman women
paras: Rome, 1st century BC-2nd century AD

The Roman woman occupied a secondary position, since she lacked political rights, so she did not vote in the assemblies or hold a magistracy, and she depended legally on her father or her husband. Her situation, however, varied greatly according to her class.
The elite woman was exempt from work, apart from household tasks, and was expected to behave in public with moral rectitude. Widows enjoyed greater freedom.
The women of the plebs, by contrast, worked in shops, workshops and markets, so a woman's free time, like a man's, depended on having someone to work for her.

Unlike the Etruscan woman, who attended banquets and competitions alongside men, the Roman woman had her presence in public restricted, and at the spectacles too. She could attend them, although with limitations, and Augustus went as far as forbidding women to attend his contests of Greek athletes, apparently because of the nudity of the athletes.

title: From agon to ludus
paras: Greece and Rome, 5th century BC-2nd century AD

There was a great difference between Greek and Roman sport. For the classical Greeks what mattered was the competition between the participants, whereas in Rome spectacle came above everything else. The Greek agon was the contest with an opponent, and the Roman ludus, the game offered to the public. Although it was originally linked to religious activities, Roman sport soon evolved into a public spectacle and an instrument of political power.
Sport in Rome was characterised, broadly speaking, by:
The perception of sport as public entertainment.
A contempt for the lives of others and a taste for violence.
The emergence of sporting professionalism and financial gain.
The development of large-scale sports facilities to favour display.
The use of sport as political control of the plebs.
The active role of the spectators during events.

title: Ludi and munera
paras: The words of Roman spectacle

The Romans had no term equivalent to our «sport», and for their games they used two words that designated different things, the ludi (plural of ludus) and the munera, each with its own origin, its own calendar and its own payer.

1. Ludi. These were the public games of the religious calendar, offered to the gods and originally paid for by the State, and they included the chariot races of the circus (ludi circenses) and theatrical performances (ludi scaenici).

2. Munus. The word meant both «duty» and «gift». Originally it was a son's obligation to his dead father, whom he honoured with a gladiatorial combat, and around the beginning of the Empire it came to designate above all the combat that a private individual offered to the people. Over time, the term was extended to all gladiatorial combats in the amphitheatres, which came to be called munera gladiatoria.

The difference between the two terms marked who decided. The ludi were public festivals with a fixed date, whereas the munus depended on the will and the purse of whoever offered it, as shown by the bags of money paid by Magerius in the mosaic on the right.

title: «Bread and circuses»
paras: Rome, 3rd century BC-4th century AD
DAYS OF PUBLIC GAMES PER YEAR

To stage the spectacles, the authorities invested a great amount of resources in building spaces capable of hosting major sporting events. This was the policy of «bread and circuses» (panem et circenses), according to which Romans were to have access to affordable food, such as the public grain, which covered around 40% of a family's basic food (Toner, 2014), and to public entertainments with which those in power won their favour.
The expression comes from the satirical poet Juvenal, who in the 2nd century AD used it as a reproach to the plebs, which once handed out commands and legions and now wanted only bread and races.

The days of public games multiplied over the course of the Empire, from 65 in the age of Augustus (27 BC-AD 14) and 80 in that of Tiberius (AD 14-37) to 176 in the calendar of AD 354, which brought together the festivals accumulated over centuries. Of these, some 102 were for theatre, 64 for races in the circus and only 10 for gladiators (see chart). Each of these spectacles rested on the same system, that is, on who paid for them, who competed and who watched.

title: Who paid for the spectacles
paras: Sporting spectacles were free for the public, and their cost fell on whoever offered and presided over them, the editor, who sought in return above all the favour of the people. As the chart above shows, that role changed from the Republic to the Empire.

Under the Republic, the games of the calendar were the responsibility of the magistrates, especially the aediles, who paid for them with public money to which they usually added their own, and for them they were an «extraordinary opportunity for electoral propaganda», since the people who enjoyed them were the same people who voted for them (Roldán, 1990).

Under the Empire, the emperor became the great sponsor. In Rome he sought to reserve the great spectacles for himself, while in the provinces they continued to be paid for by the magistrates of each city (Scheidel et al., 2007).

title: The emperor in the stands
paras: Rome and Constantinople, 1st-4th centuries AD

The emperor attended in person the games he paid for, and his presence was part of the spectacle, as the relief on the left shows, in which Theodosius appears surrounded by his court in the imperial box of the hippodrome of Constantinople. From the box, in full view of everyone, he played three roles:
that of editor of the games, organising and presiding over the event;
that of intermediary between the city and the gods, to whom the ludi were offered;
that of arbiter who granted or refused what was asked of him.

The public took advantage of that presence to clamour for what it needed, such as a reduction in the price of grain or in taxes, and the emperor had to answer there and then before tens of thousands of witnesses. Each answer strengthened or wore down his prestige.
The games thus became a space of political communication between the emperor and the people, the main place where the two met face to face.

title: 4.2.3. The amphitheatre, gladiators and other games
Amphitheatre
paras: The Roman amphitheatre was a public building with an elliptical plan, with stands all around its perimeter surrounding a central space covered with sand (harena), which gave its name to the place of combat.

The first amphitheatres arose from joining two theatres facing each other. In this way the stands completely surrounded the arena, which could be seen from any seat. They were made of wood, like the one in the Roman Forum in the reconstruction in the image, and later they were built in stone, brick and even marble, the largest reaching three or four tiers of stands one above the other.

The public entered through the vomitoria, the vaulted arches that gave access to the stands, and these rose several metres above the arena to protect the spectators from the fighters and the wild beasts.

title: Flavian Amphitheatre
paras: Colosseum
Rome, AD 72-80

The Flavian Amphitheatre, today called the Colosseum, was built between AD 72 and 80 under the Flavian dynasty. The emperor Vespasian began the works and his son Titus inaugurated it after his death with a hundred days of games.
It is one of the masterpieces of Roman architecture, and its design inspired many later amphitheatres. Its four tiers of stands surrounded an arena of some 80 by 54 metres.

Beneath the arena lay a network of corridors, cells and lifts for bringing out gladiators and wild beasts, and above the stands an enormous awning (velarium) was stretched, operated by sailors from the fleet.

The remains of its inscription suggest that it was paid for with the spoils of the Judaean war and the plunder of the Temple in Jerusalem, which is why it was at once a victory monument and a gift to the people.

title: The ordered stands
paras: Rome, from Augustus onwards

The amphitheatre audience did not sit wherever it wished. The lex Iulia theatralis, a law of Augustus (20-17 BC), allocated the seats of theatres and amphitheatres by social group, so that the stands reproduced the hierarchy of the city.

The allocation ran from bottom to top. On the podium, next to the arena, sat the emperor, in his box, and the senators; in the first tier, the equites, and in the second, the plebs, that is, the male citizens, who had to attend in a toga. The third tier was left to the poorest citizens, who could not afford a toga, together with slaves, freedmen and foreigners. Women occupied the very top, a wooden tier under the portico, separated from the rest by a wall some 5 m high.

The only women exempt from that rule were those of the imperial family, who accompanied the emperor, and the Vestals, priestesses of the goddess Vesta, who had a reserved place on the podium, next to the senators. Their privilege came from their office, since they guarded the sacred fire of the city, on which the continuity of Rome was believed to depend, and the games were, in origin, religious festivals in honour of the gods.

The figures for the Colosseum make it possible to measure that allocation (see chart). According to Bomgardner (2000), the podium and the first two tiers, reserved for senators, equites and citizens in togas, held 62% of the seats, while the third tier left 18% to the poor, slaves, freedmen and foreigners, and the wooden gallery, the furthest from the arena, 19% to women.
The dissignatores, the ushers of the amphitheatre, prevented a plebeian from occupying the reserved rows, which is why going to the games meant seeing and being seen, each in his place.

title: Gladiatorial combats
paras: Gladiatorial combats were the most prestigious spectacle of the amphitheatre and the reason why this building came to be built at all. Between the 3rd century BC and the 2nd century AD, who organised them, for what purpose and before whom they were held all changed, and that change can be followed in four stages.

At first, the combat was a private and religious act. It was organised by the family of the deceased as a munus, a son's obligation to his dead father, and its purpose was to honour the dead, hence its small scale, as the three pairs of the first combat held in Rome, in 264 BC, show.

Over time, the combat became a way of displaying the prestige of the lineage. Heirs postponed the munera and made them bigger, since a spectacular funeral showed the whole city the wealth and rank of the family, so the centre of the event shifted from the deceased to the public.

In the 1st century BC, the combat became an electoral weapon. Magistrates and candidates paid for it to win the votes of the citizens who filled the stands, and the competition between them reached such a point that the Senate had to limit the number of gladiators and forbid combats on the eve of elections.

Under the Empire, the emperor took over the great combats as his exclusive preserve. Once the people no longer voted, the spectacle came to celebrate military victories and the events of the dynasty, and thus became the main bond between the emperor and the people of Rome.

title: Gladiators and infamia
paras: Rome and the provinces, 1st century BC-2nd century AD
Gladiators came from three groups.
Slaves were bought for the arena or hired out by their owners.

The condemned. The sentence ad gladium was a death penalty carried out in the arena, without training or any chance of being spared, whereas the sentence ad ludum sent them to a gladiatorial school, where they learnt the trade and, if they survived, could obtain their discharge after a few years.

Finally, free men sold themselves voluntarily to a lanista, driven by debt, despair or, according to the Romans, madness. Impoverished former legionaries who could not adapt to civilian life were also common.

All of them shared infamia, a legal and moral stain that the law imposed on those who sold or displayed their bodies for the enjoyment of others. The infamis could not vote, hold a magistracy, testify in a trial or contract a legal marriage. It was, therefore, a social stain.

Even so, infamia was not at odds with popular admiration. Epitaphs present the gladiator with the courage, the prestige and the comradeship of the champion, and the people treated him as a hero «at once famous and infamous» (Bell, 2020).

title: The life of gladiators
paras: Gladiators lived and trained in the ludus, a school that worked at the same time as barracks, training centre and business. Private schools belonged to a lanista, an entrepreneur who bought, trained and hired out gladiators to whoever organised the games, while in Rome the great schools became imperial, like the Ludus Magnus in the image. The trade of lanista was despised, since he profited from the bodies of others, and the Romans equated him with a pimp.

Each gladiator received a combat identity (armatura), with his own weapons and way of fighting, and specialised in it with retired veterans as instructors. Physical training included lifting stones of up to 100 kg and dumbbells of 2 to 20 kg. Technical training began against a post with wooden weapons and continued in mock combats with blunt weapons, weighted to be heavier than real ones.

The diet was based on barley and pulses, with little meat, a cheap, energy-rich food, which is why gladiators were called hordearii, «barley-eaters». The bones from the gladiator cemetery at Ephesus, in present-day Turkey, confirm that diet and reveal a calcium intake higher than that of the rest of the city, which Lösch et al. (2014) attribute perhaps to a drink made from plant ash.

The school also paid for baths, massages and medical care, since the gladiator was an investment that had to be kept fit. Among the skulls from Ephesus, 16% show healed wounds, one of them with signs of surgical intervention.

title: Wives, comrades and retirement
paras: Despite the legal bar on marriage, gladiators formed families. In Hispania, 40% of the known dead had a wife, who in most cases was freeborn or a freedwoman.

Fellow members of the school also formed a community of their own. Like many humble Romans, some gladiators joined associations which, in return for a fee, guaranteed them a decent burial, and sometimes it was the troupe itself that paid for the tomb of a dead comrade.

Retirement came with the rudis, the wooden sword that symbolised discharge, or with freedom. Some veterans remained in the world of the arena as referees, instructors or even lanistae, and others, drawn by fame and money, returned to fight.

As for mortality, epitaphs give an average of ten to fifteen combats per gladiator, and for the 1st century AD Ville (1981) calculates some nineteen deaths per hundred combats. The Ephesus cemetery holds at least 68 individuals, almost all males aged 20 to 30 with an average height of 168 centimetres, the usual one in their time, so in height and age they resembled any other young Roman, and what set them apart was training.

title: How much a munus cost
paras: The chart brings together what a munus cost in AD 177, when a law of Marcus Aurelius and Commodus set the maximum price of each gladiator according to his category and the budget of the games, from 600 sesterces for a man condemned to the sword to 15,000 for a first-class gladiator in the most expensive games. That price was paid in full only if the gladiator died or was maimed, since the hire then became a purchase.

If he came back alive, the editor paid the lanista only a hire fee, around a fifth of what he was worth. Of that money the law reserved for the gladiator a quarter if he was free and a fifth if he was a slave. In the case of a first-class gladiator, what he earned was some 600-750 sesterces per combat.

Each day of games cost some 2,000 sesterces in a small city and some 50,000 in a large one. The money came from the summa honoraria, the fixed sum that each magistrate paid to the city on taking up office and that was usually spent on games, from what the editor added out of his own pocket and, at times, from public funds.
All this outlay had one ultimate aim: to win the recognition of the public by offering it free leisure and entertainment.

title: The combats
paras: A munus was announced in advance on painted notices on the walls of the city. The day followed a fixed order that built up from less to more, with the wild-beast hunts (venationes) in the morning, the execution of the condemned at midday and, in the afternoon, the main and most expensive act, the gladiatorial combats, which unfolded in six steps.
1. The eve. The night before, a great dinner open to the public was held, the cena libera, at which the gladiators could break their diet of training.
2. The entrance. The following day they paraded into the arena up to the box of the editor.
3. The inspection of the weapons. In the probatio armorum the weapons were checked and the pairs confirmed, which set different types against each other or, in some types, identical gladiators.

4. The combat. The referee, the summa rudis, watched over the duel, which lasted between 10 and 15 minutes according to Junkelmann's (2000) tests with replicas of the equipment. A gladiator who showed passivity or cowardice could be whipped or burnt with a red-hot iron by the attendants who urged them on.

5. The verdict. The loser dropped his shield and raised his index finger to ask for mercy, and the editor, attentive to the stands, decided between missio, reprieve, and iugula, the cutting of the throat.

6. The exit. The dead were carried out of the arena to the store for the bodies, where, according to Kyle (1998), they were probably routinely finished off. The Ephesus graves show 15% with a single fatal wound, which gives an idea of the survival rate in the combats.

title: Types of gladiator (I)
paras: Murmillo

Short sword, large rectangular shield and a helmet with a fish-shaped crest, which made him recognisable at a glance. He waited behind his shield until he could deliver the decisive blow, never fought another murmillo and is the type most frequent on the tombstones of the West, with 29 cases.
Thracian (thraex)

Short curved sword (sica), small shield (parma) and two high greaves. He owed his name to the Thracian warriors and reached Rome around the eighties of the 1st century BC, with Sulla's prisoners. Against the murmillo he formed the most popular pairing of the arena.
Hoplomachus

Inspired by the Greek hoplite, he carried a spear, a short sword, a small round shield of bronze and greaves up to mid-thigh, with 17-18 kg of equipment. He attacked at a distance with the spear and faced the murmillo and, at times, the Thracian, with whom he is confused because of the similar helmet.
Fans were divided between supporters of the small shield and of the large one. Even emperors took sides, Caligula with the former and Domitian with the latter.

title: Types of gladiator (II)
paras: Secutor

Smooth full helmet, with eyeholes barely three centimetres across, a large shield and 16-18 kg of equipment. His name comes from sequor, «to follow», because he pursued the retiarius without letting him cast his net, although he tired sooner. The epitaph of Flamma, a Syrian secutor, records 34 fights, with 21 victories.
Retiarius

A light gladiator, without a shield and bare-faced, with a net, trident and dagger and 7-8 kg of equipment. He retreated and circled his opponent until he gained the distance for the throw. He was one of the stars of the programme, to the point that opponents were created to suit him.
Scissor

He put his left hand into a metal cone ending in a half-moon blade, which served him both as a shield and as a weapon to cut the net. At 22 to 26 kg, he was the heaviest, although it is a poorly known type and his weight comes from modern reconstructions.

title: Types of gladiator (III)
paras: Provocator
Large shield and a breastplate over the chest (cardiophylax), with 14-15 kg. He fought against another provocator, which is why his fights were very evenly matched.
Horseman (eques)
On horseback, with a spear and a round shield, only against another eques. He brought his opponent down with the spear and finished him off on foot, and the programme usually opened with them.
Essedarius

He imitated the warriors of the light chariot of the Britons, whom Caesar encountered in 55-54 BC, and fought against another essedarius. It is debated whether he fought from the chariot or got down to fight on foot.
Archer (sagittarius)
An archer with a bow of 150 to 200 metres range, which made it necessary to protect the public. He fought against other archers and was a minority type.
A case apart, the dimachaerus (dimachaerus)
Two machetes and no shield. A programme from Pompeii announces him against a hoplomachus, and it is debated whether he was a type of his own or a way of fighting.

title: Female gladiators and huntresses
paras: Rome and the provinces, 1st-3rd centuries AD

The presence of women in the arena was regulated by the same logic as that of men, the logic of infamia, and so what concerned the Romans was their rank rather than their sex (Coleman, 2000). A rule of AD 11 barred freeborn women under the age of twenty from the arena, and ancient authors condemn only those of senatorial or equestrian family, since an elite woman who displayed herself for money dishonoured her whole lineage.

Humble women, by contrast, did fight, although always as a rarity on the programme, since the literary sources mention them fewer than ten times up to AD 200. The main evidence is the Halicarnassus relief in the image, in which Amazon and Achillia fight bare-headed, so the public knew they were women, and the inscription records that both were reprieved.

Female hunters of wild beasts were better accepted because they evoked Diana, the goddess of the hunt (Mañas, 2026), and the type survived until, in AD 200, an imperial decree forbade all women to fight.

title: Venationes
paras: The venationes were the amphitheatre spectacles with animals, from deer, wild boar or dogs to wild beasts such as lions, elephants or bears, brought from every corner of the Empire. Displaying them in Rome showed the people the reach of Roman rule over distant lands and over wild nature.

Supplying them required an organised network of capture and transport, in which professional hunters, specialised companies, the army, on the emperor's orders, and gifts from allied kings all took part, so only the richest, and above all the emperor, could gather exotic beasts in large numbers.
The spectacles took four forms, from less to more violence.
1. Display. Exotic beasts were presented to the public and sometimes performed trained.
2. Fights between beasts. The organisers set some animals against others.
3. Hunts. The venatores, professional and well-equipped hunters, killed the beasts, while the bestiarii, of lower rank, fought them with less protection.

4. Executions. Those condemned to the beasts (damnati ad bestias) died in the arena. They were always humble people, slaves, foreigners or poor free men, guilty of serious crimes such as murder, sacrilege or rebellion, since the law exempted the powerful from this penalty.

The meat of the animals was probably shared out among the spectators, and the scale of the slaughter grew with the power of whoever paid for the games, up to the 5,000 animals killed in a single day at the inauguration of the Colosseum, in AD 80.

title: Naumachiae
paras: Rome and Italy, 46 BC-AD 80

The naumachiae were naval battles with warships on lakes or in basins dug for the occasion, and their combatants were almost always condemned men or prisoners of war. Once the Colosseum was built, some were held there, in the flooded arena, such as that of Titus at its inauguration, in AD 80, which the image recreates, although how it was filled with water is still debated.

Their enormous cost reserved them for dictators and emperors, who offered them only on exceptional occasions, such as a triumph or the inauguration of a building, which is why very few are known from the first, that of Julius Caesar in 46 BC, in an artificial basin that was filled in shortly afterwards.

Their scale served to display the power of whoever paid for them. In 2 BC Augustus had a permanent basin for these combats dug on the right bank of the Tiber, fed by an aqueduct built for the purpose, which measured 533 by 355 metres, some twenty-five football pitches, allowing for the differences, and in that of Claudius on the Fucine Lake, in central Italy, 19,000 men fought in AD 52.

The combats recreated historical battles between Greeks, Persians, Phoenicians or Egyptians, and in none of the known ones did a Roman fleet fight, something Coleman (1993) attributes to the risk that Rome might lose, even in make-believe.

title: Circus
paras: Rome and the provinces, 1st century BC-4th century AD
The circus was the venue for chariot races, although on occasion it also hosted other activities such as military parades, relay races or animal hunts.

Only the main cities of the Empire built one, since it required an esplanade several hundred metres long and an expense that few cities could bear. Outside Rome fewer than sixty are known. Together with the amphitheatre and the theatre, it formed the triad of great buildings that an important city had to have to entertain the people.

The races reached Rome from Greece by way of Etruria, and Rome transformed them. In Greece they were a competition between aristocrats, won by the owner of the horses, whereas in Rome they became a spectacle that the magistrates, and later the emperor, offered to the people, with professional charioteers. For that public a renewed building arose, with large masonry stands designed to hold a great number of spectators.

The diagram on the right shows the schematic plan of the circus, a very elongated enclosure, with one straight end and one curved end. At the straight end were the starting gates (carceres), and at the curved end, the triumphal gate (porta triumphalis). Along the axis ran a low wall, the spina, which divided the track in two, and at each of its ends stood the metae, conical columns that marked the turning points of the chariots.

title: Circus Maximus
paras: Rome, 6th century BC-6th century AD

The Circus Maximus was the largest building for spectacles in Rome. It occupied the valley between the Aventine and the Palatine (two of the hills of Rome). Tradition attributes to the Etruscan kings the first stands, which were made of wood.

The venue was monumentalised over the centuries. Julius Caesar enlarged it in 46 BC with stone and marble. Augustus raised on the spina an Egyptian obelisk that now stands in the Piazza del Popolo, and Trajan rebuilt it in its final form in the 2nd century AD.

In imperial times it measured some 620 metres long by 140 wide, and its twelve carceres made it possible to line up twelve chariots side by side. Its capacity was 150,000 spectators according to Dionysius of Halicarnassus (Greek historian of the 1st century BC), a figure that Pliny the Elder (Roman naturalist of the 1st century AD) raises to 250,000.
Unlike in the amphitheatre, in the circus men and women sat together, so much so that the poet Ovid recommends it as the best place to court.
From his box, joined to the palace on the Palatine, the emperor showed himself to the people, who took advantage of the races to acclaim him or ask him for favours.

title: Chariot racing
paras: Rome and the provinces, 1st-4th centuries AD

The races almost always pitted quadrigae (4 horses) against each other, although there were also bigae (2) and trigae (3), and races with up to ten horses are known. As the turn was always to the left, the most valuable horse was the one on the far left, which ran on the inside and acted as the pivot at each turn round the meta.

The charioteer drove, like the Etruscan one, with the reins tied round his waist, so that he controlled the chariot with the weight of his body, and carried a knife to cut them if he overturned. He also had equipment that protected him in falls, with a padded helmet, a tunic with leather bands across the chest, bandages on the legs and high leather boots.

The start was given by whoever paid for the games, who dropped a white cloth from a platform above the carceres, which were arranged in an arc so that no chariot started with an advantage. Each kept to its lane as far as a white line drawn at the beginning of the spina, and then all of them made for the inside line, next to the spina. The race was seven laps, some 5 km, in eight or nine minutes. The bigae would reach a speed of 40-45 km/h and the quadrigae up to 60 km/h.

The race was decided at the turns, where the charioteer hugged the metae, and a turn taken too tight or a brush with another chariot ended in a crash. The first to cross the line received a palm and a crown, and the victory was credited to the charioteer and to his colour.

title: The circus factions
paras: Rome, 1st century BC-4th century AD

The factions (factiones) were the companies which, from the end of the Republic or the beginning of the Empire, organised the racing teams. Each one was identified with a colour, white, red, green or blue, worn by its charioteers, like the four in the mosaic in the image. Domitian added for a time gold and purple, although they were short-lived.

At the head of each was its owner (dominus factionis), an eques who ran several hundred employees, from those who looked after, held or fed the horses to vets, mechanics and carpenters. The faction kept its stables (stabula) in Rome, supplied by stud farms in Hispania, Sicily, Thessaly, North Africa and Cappadocia, and in the last centuries of the Empire it came under the control of the emperor.

On the track, the faction competed as a team. Each could enter up to three chariots in a race, so that one went for victory and the others set the pace for him or blocked the rivals on the inside line and at the turns. That is why the charioteers' inscriptions distinguish between winning from the front from the start, coming from behind or snatching victory in the final straight.

title: Charioteers and their fortunes
paras: Rome and the provinces, 1st-2nd centuries AD

Charioteers were slaves, freedmen or Romans of very low status, and of the more than two hundred known from their inscriptions only one is recorded as freeborn. Even so, the best became idols of the masses, with statues in Rome.

Each victory carried a prize paid by whoever organised the games, but it was collected by the faction, owner of the horses and the chariot, and the charioteer received only a share, which a slave could save in order to buy his freedom.

The best-documented case is that of Diocles, a freedman from Lusitania who raced from AD 122 to 146 in 4,257 races, with 1,462 victories, and retired at the age of forty-two. His inscription, an account balance in stone, records that thanks to him his faction won 35,863,120 sesterces in prizes. Diocles received a tenth of it, some three and a half million (Vamplew, 2023), almost 3,000 years of a legionary's pay and more than three times the fortune required of a senator, which is why Bell (2014) considers him perhaps the best-paid sportsman in history.

Very few got that far. Those who reached a thousand victories, the miliarii, were barely four, and the trade was as lucrative as it was dangerous, since charioteers started very young and many died in crashes. Scorpus, one of those miliarii, died at twenty-seven after more than two thousand victories, and Crescens, who won his first race at thirteen, died at twenty-two.

title: Baths
paras: Rome and the provinces, 1st century BC-4th century AD

The thermae were bathhouses in which bathing was combined with physical exercise. There were public and private ones, and the great imperial baths of Rome were decorated with marbles, statues and even libraries, like those of Caracalla.

The separation of the sexes changed over time. The oldest baths, such as those of Pompeii, had two sets of rooms, one for each sex, whereas the great imperial baths had only one, and other baths set different timetables. At the mine of Vipasca (Portugal, 2nd century AD), women bathed in the morning and men in the afternoon. Even so, Ward (1992) finds mixed bathing up to the 4th century.
The baths served for hygiene, relaxation and social life. Entry cost a quadrans, the smallest coin, so anyone could afford it, as the image recreates.

The baths were also a noisy and rather disorderly place. People ate and drank there, as shown by a graffito from Herculaneum that notes food prices in asses, there were fights and crowds, and some graffiti recall that people also sought sex and that prostitution was practised. The most frequent problem was the theft of clothes, which bathers left in the changing room in the care of a slave, which is why at the baths of Bath (Britannia) curse tablets against thieves were found (Fagan, 1999).

title: The rooms of the baths
paras: Rome, 1st-3rd centuries AD

The diagram follows the bather's route through an imperial bathhouse. He left his clothes in the apodyterium, the changing room, in small niches watched over by a slave, and went out into the palaestra, the porticoed courtyard where exercise before bathing took place. There people lifted weights, practised wrestling and played ball games.

After exercise he sweated in the laconicum, the steam room, moved on to the caldarium, with its tubs of hot water, went back to the tepidarium, a transitional room, and finished in the frigidarium, with those of cold water.

Ball games were common in the baths. The Greek physician Galen (2nd century AD) devoted an entire treatise, On exercise with the small ball (Galen, 1997), to defending this game as the best bodily activity. According to him, it moved the whole body with whatever intensity one wished, suited any age and cost hardly any money, so it was within the reach even of the poor. Moreover, unlike wrestling, it also trained the mind, because it forced the player to anticipate the opponent's movements, and it rarely caused injuries.

title: Roman balls
paras: Rome, 1st-2nd centuries AD

Pila paganica. This was the most common ball, stuffed with feathers, and it was played by keeping it from falling or passing it with or without a bounce. The poet Martial describes it as neither as soft as the follis nor as hard as the ordinary pila, and the one in the upper image is a modern reconstruction.

Follis. This was a larger ball, of inflated skin, very light and suited to children and the elderly, like the one in the drawing in the lower image. It was made from an inflated pig's bladder covered with leather, and children warmed it by the fire to round it out. Even so, adults used it too, and Augustus, after the civil wars, exchanged exercises with weapons for the ball and the follis.

title: Trigon and harpastum
paras: Rome, 1st-5th centuries AD

Pila trigonalis. A popular game in which three players (trigonali) stood forming a triangle (trigon). The idea was to pass a small ball hard to test the reflexes of a team-mate, who had to catch it without letting it fall, and perhaps several balls at once were used. In wealthy houses the slaves who were given the name of pilicrepus replaced the balls and kept count of the points.
The trigon · Author's elaboration based on Fagan (2021)

Harpastum. It was played with a small, hard and somewhat heavy ball. A player standing in the middle tried to intercept the ball that the others passed to one another, a game that required speed and reflexes. Some women also played it, among them Philaenis, whom the poet Martial mocks.

Another variant, of great physical violence, was played in teams. It consisted of carrying the ball towards the opponents' goal, and tackles, blows, feints and dribbles were allowed. It was so popular that it became part of the physical training of the Roman legions.

title: Athletics in Rome
paras: Rome, 186 BC-3rd century AD

Greek athletics reached Rome in 186 BC, when a victorious general offered, according to the historian Livy, the first contest of athletes brought from Greece together with a hunt of lions and panthers. During the Republic it was an occasional display among other spectacles that the Roman watched from the stands, since undressing before one's fellow citizens was considered shameful.

The emperor Domitian (AD 81-96) gave it a home of its own with this stadium, built for the Capitoline Games, a Greek-style contest that he instituted in AD 86, held every four years and, according to the biographer Suetonius, included a girls' race. It was the first permanent stadium in Rome, with some 30,000 spectators.

The shape of the building recalled that of a smaller circus (right-hand image). The track measured some 192 metres, the length of the Greek stadium, and besides athletics it hosted boxing, pankration and, probably, gladiators after the fire in the Colosseum in AD 217. Its site is now occupied by Piazza Navona, which preserves its shape.

Women playing ball appear above all in a mosaic from the Villa del Casale, at Piazza Armerina (Sicily), from the first half of the 4th century AD (left-hand image), which decorated a room in the private part of the villa. Even so, women's sport was an uncommon practice in Rome, since a woman exercising outside the home was considered improper.

The girls in the mosaic wear briefs and a band across the chest, the strophium, with which sportswomen covered themselves, which is why popular accounts have called them the «bikini girls» (Muñoz-Santos, 2017). Some play ball, and others run, throw the discus or prepare for the jump with halteres, while the winners receive the palm and the crown of victory.

The scene was at first taken for a beauty contest and is today interpreted as an athletic competition (Pensabene & Gallocchio, 2011). Together with the girls' race at the Capitoline Games and the female fighters of the arena, it shows that women did compete in Rome, although almost always in private settings or as a rarity on the programme, and in the events of Greek athletics, the foot race, the jump and the discus.

title: How the spectacles faded away
paras: West and East, 4th-6th centuries AD

Roman spectacles were not banned in any particular year. In the West no law put an end to them, so each spectacle followed its own chronology. Gladiatorial combats were the first to disappear: by the end of the 4th century they took up in Rome only ten days in December, and the last was probably held c. 440.

The spectacles also had their critics. Pagan moralists, such as Cicero and Seneca, condemned cruelty towards those who could not defend themselves and urged the educated man not to let himself be carried away by the crowd, while Christian writers, such as Tertullian, rejected them as idolatry, since everything in them was consecrated to the pagan gods.

The main cause was money. From the 3rd century the cities grew poorer, and the rich who had once paid for the games devoted their generosity to churches, hospitals and almsgiving, which the bishops presented as the new way to earn recognition. Jiménez Sánchez (2002) considers the weight of Christianity exaggerated and puts cost first, since gladiatorial combat was the most expensive spectacle. Stocking (2021) agrees that Christianity was not the main cause.

Hunts and races, cheaper and more popular, lasted longer. After the fall of the Western Empire in 476, the Germanic kings of Italy kept up the games, and there the last documented hunt dates from 523 and the last race from 549.

In the East, by contrast, the emperor went on paying, and the hippodrome of Constantinople kept up the races and the factions for centuries (Giatsis, 2000; Parnell, 2014). The spectacle was a service paid for by those in power, and it faded out wherever they stopped paying for it.

title: The functions of Roman sport and its legacy
paras: Throughout the topic, Roman sport has appeared linked to four spheres of city life, power, the social order, religion and health, and in all of them the distance from the Greek agon can be seen, because in Rome the game offered to the public took precedence over competition between the participants.

First, sport served power. The elite offered games to the plebs on a regular and free basis to win its favour, the rich man who paid for them received recognition in return (euergetism) and the emperor showed himself in the stands as the one who gave the games and granted what was asked of him.

Second, sport ordered society, since the stands reproduced the hierarchy of the city and whoever displayed himself for money was branded with infamia, which is why in the arena and the circus those who competed were above all slaves, the condemned and professionals while the citizen watched from the stands, as in Etruria.
Thirdly, it was a rite, since the ludi belonged to the religious calendar and the circus remained a sacred space, which is why the Christians condemned it.
Finally, everyday exercise served health in the baths, open to anyone for a token price, and in ball games, whose benefits Galen defended.

The hippodrome of Constantinople kept the races going in the East, but what passed into the Middle Ages was above all the practices that needed no one to pay for them. The warrior aristocracy of the Germanic kingdoms kept hunting and exercises on horseback as preparation for war and a sign of rank, the common people kept ball games and games of strength at their festivals, and the Church, which had condemned the spectacle, came to set the festive calendar. Sport ceased to be a spectacle that the city offered to the stands and became a group practice, that of the nobles, that of the peasants and that of the clergy.
